symptom: Squeaky tread when walked on
customer_language: the stairs creak when I walk on them

possible_causes.cause: Loose tread-to-string joint
possible_causes.why: The tread has lifted slightly out of its housing in the string and rubs on each step.

possible_causes.cause: Failed wedge under the tread
possible_causes.why: The pine wedge that locks the tread into the string housing has dried out or fallen away.

possible_causes.cause: Loose glue block at tread-riser corner
possible_causes.why: The angle block glued behind the joint has failed and the joint now flexes under load.

possible_causes.cause: Nosing rubbing on riser above
possible_causes.why: Seasonal timber movement has closed the gap; the two surfaces rub.

diagnostic_questions.q: Is the squeak worse in winter (when heating is on)?
Can you see a visible gap between the tread and the riser above it?

repair_options.method: Access the underside of the stair if possible. Apply wood glue into the gap between tread and string. Wedge or screw upward from below to close the joint. Clamp until dry.
From underneath, remove the loose wedge, apply glue, drive a new pine wedge into the housing to tighten the tread. Cut off protruding wedge flush.

repair_options.for_cause: Loose glue block at tread-riser corner
repair_options.method: From underneath, re-glue any loose angle blocks. Add a new 60mm block with wood glue if the original is missing.

when_to_call_professional: If the stair has no accessible underside (closed under-stair storage), or if multiple treads squeak, call an installer to diagnose whether the whole flight needs re-wedging.

symptom: Multiple treads squeak in cold weather
customer_language: noisier when the heating is on

possible_causes.cause: Seasonal timber shrinkage opening joint gaps
possible_causes.why: Central heating dries the timber; gaps open at every joint and squeak under load.

possible_causes.cause: Insufficient wedging at manufacture
possible_causes.why: Marginal wedges only reveal themselves when shrinkage removes the last of the friction.

diagnostic_questions.q: Do the squeaks disappear again in summer?

repair_options.for_cause: Seasonal timber shrinkage opening joint gaps
repair_options.method: Add a humidifier in the hallway during heating season to keep relative humidity above 40%. Squeaks typically reduce within 2-3 weeks.
Installer re-wedges from underneath - not a homeowner job.

when_to_call_professional: If squeaks persist through spring and summer, the cause is structural not seasonal - call an installer.

symptom: Newel post creaks when handrail is pressed
customer_language: post at the bottom of the stairs makes a noise

possible_causes.cause: Loose newel base fixing
possible_causes.why: The bolt or screw fixing the newel to the floor structure has slackened; movement produces the creak.

possible_causes.cause: Failed mortice-and-tenon joint at string
possible_causes.why: The string tenon in the newel mortice has dried and shrunk; the joint creaks under lateral load.

diagnostic_questions.q: Does the newel visibly rock when you push it sideways?

repair_options.method: Access the fixing (may be under floorboards or in the newel base). Tighten the bolt or replace short screws with longer structural screws. Add wood glue at the joint face.
Requires bench-joinery repair - installer to re-fix with hidden reinforcement.

when_to_call_professional: If tightening the visible fixings does not stop the creak, call an installer - a loose newel is a handrail-safety issue.

symptom: Spindles rattle when someone walks past

possible_causes.cause: Loose slips in the baserail or handrail groove
possible_causes.why: The infill slips between spindles have shrunk or come loose; spindles now have play in the groove.

possible_causes.cause: Spindle shrinkage in the groove
possible_causes.why: Timber shrinkage has left the spindle loose in its housing.

diagnostic_questions.q: Can you push a spindle sideways with your finger and see it move?

repair_options.for_cause: Loose slips in the baserail or handrail groove
repair_options.method: Remove the loose slip, apply wood glue, refit and pin with 23-gauge headless pin. Touch up any visible pin hole with filler.
Insert a small hardwood wedge into the groove alongside the spindle, glue and trim flush.

when_to_call_professional: If more than a few spindles are loose, call an installer - could indicate a wider balustrade fixing issue.

symptom: Ticking noise from stairs at night

possible_causes.cause: Thermal expansion and contraction of timber
possible_causes.why: The heating cycles on/off; timber components expand and contract at joints producing the tick.

possible_causes.cause: Pipe or heating system passing under stairs
possible_causes.why: The tick is from the pipework, not the stairs themselves.

diagnostic_questions.q: Does the ticking follow the heating cycle (on/off)?

repair_options.for_cause: Thermal expansion and contraction of timber
repair_options.method: Normal seasonal behaviour, no repair needed. Educating the household usually resolves the concern.

when_to_call_professional: If ticking becomes loud cracking or is accompanied by visible movement, call an installer.

symptom: Deep groan under weight in the middle of a flight
customer_language: stairs groan when I walk up

possible_causes.cause: Under-supported stringer flexing under load
possible_causes.why: The stringer is spanning too far without midspan support and flexes noticeably.

possible_causes.cause: Missing or failed midspan bracket
possible_causes.why: A midspan support bracket has come away from the wall.

diagnostic_questions.q: Can you see the stair visibly deflect (dip) when someone walks up it?

repair_options.method: Requires structural assessment and installation of intermediate support - installer only.
Installer re-fixes bracket into structural wall behind.

when_to_call_professional: Immediately. Visible deflection on a domestic stair indicates structural inadequacy.
safety_note: If deflection is visible during use, limit stair use to essential trips only until inspected.

symptom: Squeak only on top step

possible_causes.cause: Top nosing not fixed to landing
possible_causes.why: The final tread nosing extends onto the landing floor but was never secured to it.

possible_causes.cause: Landing board loose at stair connection
possible_causes.why: The landing floorboard closest to the stair top has come loose from the trimmer joist.

diagnostic_questions.q: Can you feel the landing board move when you press it?

repair_options.for_cause: Top nosing not fixed to landing
repair_options.method: Screw the top nosing down into the landing joist with two hidden countersunk screws, filled and finished.

repair_options.for_cause: Landing board loose at stair connection
repair_options.method: Locate the joist through the loose board, fix with 60mm screws countersunk and filled.

when_to_call_professional: If unclear which board is moving, or the whole landing feels bouncy, call an installer.

symptom: Handrail creaks when gripped hard
customer_language: rail makes noise when I lean on it

possible_causes.cause: Loose handrail-to-newel joint
possible_causes.why: The screw or bolt joining handrail to newel has slackened; the joint creaks under lateral load.

possible_causes.cause: Failed handrail wall bracket
possible_causes.why: A wall bracket has come loose in the plaster or fixings.

diagnostic_questions.q: Does the creak come from a specific point along the handrail?

repair_options.method: Access the joint fixing (may be through the newel top under a cap). Tighten the bolt, or add a hidden reinforcement screw. See loose-handrail entries for detail.
Remove bracket cover, replace short screws with longer structural screws into stud or masonry with correct plugs.

when_to_call_professional: If tightening does not stop the creak, or fixings pull straight out, call an installer.

symptom: Squeak from the bottom step only

possible_causes.cause: Bullnose starting step not properly bedded on subfloor
possible_causes.why: The starting step rests on an uneven subfloor without packers - flexes under load.

possible_causes.cause: Loose fixing to lower newel
possible_causes.why: The starting step joint to the newel has come loose.

diagnostic_questions.q: Does the step feel like it moves as a whole unit, or just at one edge?

repair_options.for_cause: Bullnose starting step not properly bedded on subfloor
repair_options.method: Lift the step or access from below if possible. Insert timber or plastic packers to bring it into solid contact with the subfloor. Refix.
Locate and tighten the newel-to-step fixing, or add a hidden reinforcement.

when_to_call_professional: If the step cannot be lifted safely, or the newel itself rocks, call an installer.

symptom: Squeak that moves depending on where you step
customer_language: different squeaks all over the stairs

possible_causes.cause: General wedging failure across the whole flight
possible_causes.why: The pine wedges under multiple treads have dried and released - the stair flexes at every joint.

possible_causes.cause: Insufficient original fixing across the flight
possible_causes.why: The staircase was under-fixed at installation; wear over time has revealed it.

diagnostic_questions.q: Is the staircase more than 20 years old?

repair_options.for_cause: General wedging failure across the whole flight
repair_options.method: Full re-wedge from underneath - installer job. Access via under-stair area; every joint refreshed with glue and new pine wedges.

repair_options.for_cause: Insufficient original fixing across the flight
repair_options.method: Installer assessment - may need refurbishment rather than repair.

when_to_call_professional: Yes - a whole-flight squeak pattern is not a homeowner-DIY job.

symptom: Newel post wobbles when pushed sideways
customer_language: post moves when I push it

possible_causes.cause: Loose bolt or screw at newel base
possible_causes.why: The structural fixing to the floor or joist has slackened.

possible_causes.cause: Rotten timber at floor line
possible_causes.why: Moisture damage (often historic) has weakened the timber the newel is fixed into.

possible_causes.cause: Wedges below newel base failed
possible_causes.why: Original pine wedges have released, newel is no longer bedded solidly.

diagnostic_questions.q: Is there visible water staining or soft timber at the newel base?

repair_options.for_cause: Loose bolt or screw at newel base
repair_options.method: Access fixing, tighten or upgrade to longer structural screw. Add glue at the joint face if bench-accessible.
Structural repair by installer - remove rotten section and splice new timber, or replace newel.
Installer re-wedges the newel base from below.

when_to_call_professional: A loose newel is a handrail-safety issue. Fix within days, not weeks.
safety_note: Warn all household members not to lean on the handrail heavily until the newel is re-secured.

symptom: Handrail feels loose but I can't tell where

possible_causes.cause: Loose newel post transmitting movement to handrail
possible_causes.why: The newel is loose; the handrail attached to it inherits the movement.

possible_causes.cause: Handrail-to-newel joint has failed
possible_causes.why: The bolt or screw holding handrail to newel has come loose.

possible_causes.cause: Wall bracket has failed
possible_causes.why: The bracket fixing to the wall has come away from the substrate.

diagnostic_questions.q: Walk the handrail slowly and press each section - where does it move?

repair_options.method: See loose-newel diagnostic (diag-011).
See loose-handrail repair options in brain entries 1804 and 1806.
Longer screws into structural wall; correct plugs for substrate.

when_to_call_professional: If diagnostic push-test does not identify the source, or the customer is uncomfortable working at height on the stair.
safety_note: A wobbly handrail is a safety-critical defect - do not use it as primary support until repaired.

symptom: Landing bounces underfoot

possible_causes.cause: Insufficient joists or missing noggins
possible_causes.why: Landing framing spans too far without lateral bracing - deflects noticeably.

possible_causes.cause: Landing boards too thin for the span
possible_causes.why: Undersized boards flex individually even if the joists are correct.

possible_causes.cause: Poor fixing to joists
possible_causes.why: Screws missed the joists at installation.

diagnostic_questions.q: Does the whole landing move together, or just individual boards?

repair_options.method: Structural repair - additional joists or noggins added from below. Installer or structural carpenter.
Replace boards with correct-thickness stock.
Locate joists and re-fix boards with correct-length structural screws.

when_to_call_professional: Landing bounce on a new install is a defect the installer must fix. On older stairs, get structural inspection before use as heavy access route.
safety_note: If the bounce is increasing over time, or accompanied by cracking sounds, stop use and inspect immediately.

symptom: Whole staircase moves as one unit

possible_causes.cause: Failed fixing at top or bottom of stringers
possible_causes.why: The stair is no longer positively connected to the floor structure at one end.

possible_causes.cause: Structural failure of trimmer joist
possible_causes.why: The joist that carries the top of the stair has failed or split.

diagnostic_questions.q: Can you see or feel gaps opening between the stair top and the landing?

repair_options.for_cause: Failed fixing at top or bottom of stringers
repair_options.method: Installer to re-fix stringers to the structure with correct bolts or structural screws.
Structural carpenter or engineer - the joist needs strengthening or replacing.

when_to_call_professional: Immediately.
safety_note: Do not use the staircase until inspected. Use an alternative route between floors.

symptom: Individual spindle can be pulled out by hand

possible_causes.cause: Failed slip fixing
possible_causes.why: The infill slips that lock the spindle in the baserail/handrail groove have come out.

possible_causes.cause: Original glue joint failure
possible_causes.why: The glue at the top or bottom of the spindle has released with age or timber movement.

diagnostic_questions.q: Are the slips between spindles missing or loose?

repair_options.method: Refit spindle in groove, glue and refit slips either side with wood glue and 23-gauge pins.
Apply wood glue to both ends of spindle, refit into grooves, pin discreetly to hold while glue cures.

when_to_call_professional: If more than 2-3 spindles are loose, or if the whole balustrade feels weak.
safety_note: A missing spindle is a fall risk - warn children and cover the gap until repaired.

symptom: Tread visibly rocks when stepped on

possible_causes.cause: Front nosing fixing failed
possible_causes.why: The tread has lost its fixing at the front edge and pivots on the back.

possible_causes.cause: Tread lifted from string housing
possible_causes.why: The tread has come out of its housing in the string on one or both sides.

diagnostic_questions.q: Can you see a gap under the tread nosing when weight is off it?

repair_options.method: Screw down through the nosing into the riser below with countersunk screws, filled and finished.
Installer to re-seat and re-wedge from underneath.

when_to_call_professional: A rocking tread is a trip hazard - fix within days, not weeks.
safety_note: Avoid the affected step until repaired if possible.

symptom: Glass balustrade panel wobbles in its channel

possible_causes.cause: Glass gasket or rubber setting has failed
possible_causes.why: The rubber setting that grips the glass in the channel has degraded or dropped out.

possible_causes.cause: Channel fixings to stair have loosened
possible_causes.why: The channel itself is no longer solidly fixed to the stair.

diagnostic_questions.q: Is the glass loose in the channel, or is the channel itself loose?

repair_options.for_cause: Glass gasket or rubber setting has failed
repair_options.method: Specialist glass installer replaces gasket - not a DIY job because glass handling is unforgiving.

repair_options.for_cause: Channel fixings to stair have loosened
repair_options.method: Installer re-fixes channel and re-seats glass.

when_to_call_professional: Immediately - loose glass on a stair is a serious safety issue.
safety_note: Do not lean on the glass panel until repaired. If children are in the household, restrict access to the stair.

symptom: Handrail cap on top of newel is loose

possible_causes.cause: Glue on cap has failed
possible_causes.why: The cap is normally glued and pinned to the newel top; glue can release over time.

diagnostic_questions.q: Does the cap lift straight off, or just wobble?

repair_options.method: Remove cap, scrape old glue off both faces, re-glue with wood glue, clamp for 4 hours. Optional: add a discreet pin from the side.

when_to_call_professional: Only if the newel post itself is also loose (see diag-011).

symptom: Riser board rattles when a tread is stepped on

possible_causes.cause: Riser has come loose from tread groove above
possible_causes.why: The riser tongue that fits into the groove under the tread has released.

possible_causes.cause: Angle blocks behind riser failed
possible_causes.why: The angle blocks that reinforce the tread-to-riser joint have failed.

diagnostic_questions.q: Can you push the riser inward with a finger and feel it move?

answer_maps_to.Yes: Riser loose from tread or blocks

repair_options.for_cause: Riser has come loose from tread groove above
repair_options.method: From underneath, apply glue and re-secure with angle blocks or a fixing into the tread.
From underneath, re-glue any loose blocks or add new 60mm angle blocks with wood glue.

when_to_call_professional: If underside is not accessible.

symptom: Whole balustrade panel section moves as one

possible_causes.cause: Newel fixing at one end has failed
possible_causes.why: One of the newels bracketing the panel is loose; whole balustrade transmits the movement.

possible_causes.cause: Baserail or handrail fixing has failed
possible_causes.why: The horizontal members are no longer fixed to the newel at one end.

diagnostic_questions.q: Which newel is loose - top, bottom, or both?

repair_options.for_cause: Newel fixing at one end has failed
repair_options.method: See loose-newel repair (diag-011).

repair_options.for_cause: Baserail or handrail fixing has failed
repair_options.method: Tighten or replace fixings between horizontal member and newel.

when_to_call_professional: If the whole flight moves (both newels loose), stop use and call an installer immediately.
safety_note: Balustrade is a fall prevention system - a loose panel is a safety-critical defect.

symptom: Cracked riser board

possible_causes.cause: Impact damage
possible_causes.why: Something has struck the riser - vacuum, footwear, moving furniture.

possible_causes.cause: Timber movement crack
possible_causes.why: Seasonal shrinkage has cracked a wide solid-timber riser.

diagnostic_questions.q: Is the crack a clean split, or splintered?

repair_options.method: Small cracks: fill with matching wood filler, sand, touch up finish. Large cracks: replace the riser.
Fill with wood filler that accepts finish. Prime and paint if painted; touch up lacquer if clear-finished.

when_to_call_professional: If the riser needs replacing (rather than filling) - fitting a new painted or veneer-matched riser is a joinery job.

symptom: Split at end of a tread

possible_causes.cause: Wedge behind tread has forced the timber to split
possible_causes.why: Over-driven wedge has caused a longitudinal split along the tread.

possible_causes.cause: Over-fixing at manufacture
possible_causes.why: Screw too close to the edge has split the timber.

diagnostic_questions.q: Is the split at the front nosing or at the back (against the riser above)?

repair_options.method: Glue and clamp the split closed with a sash clamp. Fill hairline residue. Refinish.
Consider replacing the tread - a split nosing under load is a safety issue.

when_to_call_professional: If the split extends across more than half the tread width, or the tread flexes under load.
safety_note: A split tread near the nosing is a fall risk - avoid the step if possible until inspected.

symptom: Newel cap has split
customer_language: cap on top of post cracked

possible_causes.cause: Timber shrinkage in the cap
possible_causes.why: Solid-timber cap has cracked as it dried out with central heating.

possible_causes.cause: Impact damage
possible_causes.why: Something struck the cap.

repair_options.method: Fill crack with wood filler, sand, refinish. Or replace the cap with a new matching one.
Fill and refinish, or replace.

when_to_call_professional: If the cap is one-of-a-kind or matching new caps is difficult.

symptom: Dented or crushed tread nosing

possible_causes.cause: Impact damage (dropped object)
possible_causes.why: Heavy object dropped on the nosing.

possible_causes.cause: Furniture moving damage
possible_causes.why: Furniture edge dragged across the nosing.

repair_options.method: Small dents: steam-raise the fibre with damp cloth and hot iron, then sand smooth and refinish. Deep dents: fill with matching wood filler.

when_to_call_professional: If the whole nosing needs replacing, or the tread is a hardwood with complex grain matching.

symptom: Water stain on tread

possible_causes.cause: Spilled water penetrated finish
possible_causes.why: Water sat on the tread long enough to penetrate the lacquer or oil.

possible_causes.cause: Historic leak from above
possible_causes.why: Water damage from an old plumbing leak.

diagnostic_questions.q: Is the stain from a recent spill or from historic damage?

repair_options.method: Light stain: sand with 240 grit, refinish. Deep stain: oxalic-acid stain remover, then sand and refinish. Test in inconspicuous area first.

when_to_call_professional: If stain is deep, wide, or the tread has bowed from water damage.

symptom: Rot at bottom of stringer or newel

possible_causes.cause: Long-term moisture ingress at floor level
possible_causes.why: Water tracking under skirting or from an old leak has rotted the timber over years.

possible_causes.cause: Direct water contact (external stairs)
possible_causes.why: External or partially external stair exposed to rain.

diagnostic_questions.q: Can you push a screwdriver into the timber easily?

repair_options.for_cause: Long-term moisture ingress or direct water contact
repair_options.method: Structural repair by carpenter - cut back to sound timber and splice in new section, or replace whole component. Address the moisture source first or the repair will fail again.

when_to_call_professional: Immediately - rot in a load-bearing component is a structural failure risk.
safety_note: Do not use the staircase for heavy loads until inspected. Identify and stop the water source before repair.

symptom: Deep scratch across a tread

possible_causes.cause: Furniture or heavy object dragged
possible_causes.why: Sharp edge dragged across the finish.

possible_causes.cause: Pet claws or shoe damage
possible_causes.why: Repeated wear at a specific location.

diagnostic_questions.q: Is the scratch through the finish only, or into the wood?

repair_options.method: Light scratch: rub with matching-colour wax stick. Deep scratch: fill with wood filler colour-matched to species, sand, refinish that area.
Same repair; consider protective runner or nosing strip in high-wear areas.

when_to_call_professional: If the whole tread needs refinishing, or the scratch pattern indicates the finish is generally failing.

symptom: Chip out of glass balustrade edge

possible_causes.cause: Impact damage (usually during furniture move)
possible_causes.why: Object struck the glass edge.

possible_causes.cause: Manufacturing defect revealing under load
possible_causes.why: Latent edge damage from cutting has propagated.

diagnostic_questions.q: Is the chip on the edge only, or has a crack propagated into the face?

repair_options.method: Glass panels cannot be repaired - replace the panel. Specialist glass supplier with the original spec.

when_to_call_professional: Immediately. A chipped edge can propagate into full panel failure.
safety_note: Toughened glass fails suddenly and completely. Do not lean on the affected panel until replaced.

symptom: Handrail surface has become rough

possible_causes.cause: Finish has worn through in high-touch areas
possible_causes.why: Years of hand contact has worn the lacquer or oil away.

possible_causes.cause: UV damage from strong direct sunlight
possible_causes.why: Sun exposure has degraded the finish.

repair_options.for_cause: Finish worn through or UV damage
repair_options.method: Light sand with 240 grit along the grain, clean thoroughly, apply matching finish. Oil finishes are easier to spot-repair than lacquer.

when_to_call_professional: If the whole handrail needs refinishing, or a lacquer finish is desired (spray application).

symptom: Small burn mark on tread

possible_causes.cause: Cigarette or hot object contact
possible_causes.why: Something hot rested on the finish.

repair_options.method: Light burn: sand out with 240 grit and refinish. Deep burn (into wood): drill out, fill with matching filler, sand and refinish.

when_to_call_professional: If the burn is deep and species matching is difficult (e.g. walnut).

symptom: Split at end of skirting where it meets stair string

possible_causes.cause: Poor original mitre or scribe
possible_causes.why: The joint was never neat because it was not planned pre-manufacture (see brain entry 1838).

possible_causes.cause: Timber movement has opened joint
possible_causes.why: Seasonal movement has opened a joint that was originally tight.

repair_options.for_cause: Poor original mitre or timber movement
repair_options.method: Fill gap with decorator's caulk (paintable acrylic) matched to the paint colour. Simple cosmetic fix.

when_to_call_professional: If the join is fundamentally wrong (skirting cuts against a string that was not prepared) - carpenter to rework the detail.

symptom: Loose or missing nail head on tread surface

possible_causes.cause: Original pin fixing has worked loose
possible_causes.why: Timber movement has ejected the pin.

possible_causes.cause: Under-driven pin at manufacture
possible_causes.why: Original fixing was never fully seated.

repair_options.for_cause: Original pin fixing has worked loose
repair_options.method: Punch the pin below the surface with a nail punch. Fill the hole with matching wood filler. Refinish that spot.

when_to_call_professional: If multiple pins are working out across the flight - indicates a wider fixing issue.
safety_note: A protruding pin is a foot injury risk - repair the same day if barefoot use is normal.

symptom: Peeling paint on stringer

possible_causes.cause: Poor surface preparation at original paint
possible_causes.why: The stringer was not primed or sanded properly before painting.

possible_causes.cause: Wrong paint type over unsuitable substrate
possible_causes.why: Waterborne paint applied over old oil-based paint without correct primer.

repair_options.for_cause: Poor prep or wrong paint type
repair_options.method: Scrape peeling paint back to solid edge. Sand smooth. Apply appropriate primer (adhesion primer if unsure of substrate). Re-paint with 2 coats of quality water-based satin or eggshell.

when_to_call_professional: If large areas are affected, or the paint is coming off in sheets.

symptom: Faded stain on tread edges

possible_causes.cause: UV damage from window sunlight
possible_causes.why: Direct sunlight over months or years has bleached the stain.

possible_causes.cause: Wear from foot traffic on stain-only finish
possible_causes.why: Stain alone with no protective topcoat wears with use.

repair_options.method: Light sand, apply matching stain to blend, then apply UV-resistant topcoat (hardwax oil with UV inhibitor, or UV-protective lacquer).

when_to_call_professional: If the whole flight needs re-staining (large job, better with spray gun and controlled environment).

symptom: Sticky varnish finish

possible_causes.cause: Finish never fully cured
possible_causes.why: Applied too thick, or in wrong temperature / humidity - finish did not cross-link fully.

possible_causes.cause: Household cleaner has reacted with finish
possible_causes.why: Wrong cleaning product has left a sticky residue.

diagnostic_questions.q: Was the finish applied recently, or has it been fine for years and just become sticky?

repair_options.method: Sand back to bare timber and refinish - uncured finish cannot be recovered by adding more.

repair_options.for_cause: Household cleaner has reacted with finish
repair_options.method: Wipe with white spirit on a rag, then clean with mild soapy water. Test on inconspicuous area first.

when_to_call_professional: If the finish needs stripping and reapplying.

symptom: White ring or watermark on lacquered tread

possible_causes.cause: Moisture trapped under lacquer
possible_causes.why: Water sat long enough to penetrate the finish and become trapped in the microstructure.

repair_options.method: Cover with cloth and apply hot iron for a few seconds at a time - heat draws moisture out. If persistent, light sand and refinish that patch.

when_to_call_professional: If deep water has bowed the timber underneath.

symptom: Yellow discolouration in white paint

possible_causes.cause: Oil-based paint yellowing with age (normal)
possible_causes.why: Oil-based whites yellow over years, especially in low-light areas.

possible_causes.cause: Tannin bleed from underlying timber
possible_causes.why: Oak tannins have bled through inadequate primer.

diagnostic_questions.q: Is the yellowing worse in shadow areas or on oak substrate?

repair_options.method: Sand lightly, prime with stain-block primer, repaint with modern water-based white (does not yellow).
Sand back to primer, apply oil-based stain-block primer, then repaint.

when_to_call_professional: If the whole staircase needs stripping.

symptom: Oil finish looking dry and thirsty

possible_causes.cause: Normal wear - oil needs periodic refresh
possible_causes.why: Hardwax oil and Danish oil need re-application every 2-5 years in high-wear areas.

repair_options.method: Clean thoroughly, light key with 240 grit, apply thin coat of matching oil with lint-free cloth. Wipe off excess. Cure 12 hours.

when_to_call_professional: Not usually - oil refresh is one of the easiest maintenance jobs.

symptom: Visible glue squeeze-out on finished timber

possible_causes.cause: Installer did not clean glue before finish
possible_causes.why: Wood glue left on timber blocks finish absorption - shows as different colour patch.

repair_options.method: Sand back to bare timber in the affected area, apply matching finish. Small patches blend well; large patches show.

when_to_call_professional: If this is on a new installation - it is an installer defect they should return to correct under warranty.

symptom: Uneven sheen across the finish

possible_causes.cause: Inadequate sanding before finish
possible_causes.why: Different sanding grits absorbed finish differently - the pattern shows through.

possible_causes.cause: Finish applied in different conditions
possible_causes.why: Some sections applied at different temperature or humidity, cured to different sheen.

repair_options.method: Best fixed by full re-sand and consistent re-application - spray-booth finish is more consistent than brush.

when_to_call_professional: Yes, unless the customer is happy to live with the patchiness. Full refinish is a workshop-level job.

symptom: Sun damage on treads near a stairwell window

possible_causes.cause: UV bleaching of timber and finish
possible_causes.why: Direct sunlight over years bleaches natural timber colour and degrades finish.

repair_options.method: Sand back to bare timber, apply UV-protective finish (UV-inhibitor oil or UV lacquer). Prevention: window film or blinds on the stairwell window.

when_to_call_professional: Full flight refinish is a workshop-level job.

symptom: Filler visible under paint on riser

possible_causes.cause: Filler was not primed before top coat
possible_causes.why: Filler absorbs paint differently to timber - shows as a patch unless primed.

repair_options.method: Prime the whole riser with a decent primer, then two coats of finish paint.

when_to_call_professional: If this is on a new install, the decorator should return to correct.

symptom: Stringer sagging visibly along the flight

possible_causes.cause: Undersized stringer for the span
possible_causes.why: The stringer was too thin or shallow for the flight length; it has deflected over years of load.

possible_causes.cause: Rot or insect damage reducing structural section
possible_causes.why: Hidden rot has weakened the stringer.

diagnostic_questions.q: Is the sag more than 15mm across the flight?

repair_options.method: Structural repair by carpenter or engineer - additional stringer added, or full replacement.

when_to_call_professional: Immediately.
safety_note: A sagging stringer is a structural failure. Stop use until inspected.

symptom: Crack across landing near stair head
customer_language: split in floorboard at top of stairs

possible_causes.cause: Under-supported landing joist
possible_causes.why: The joist has flexed past its elastic limit and cracked.

possible_causes.cause: Impact damage or historic overload
possible_causes.why: Something heavy has been dropped or a very heavy object was moved across the landing.

diagnostic_questions.q: Is the crack in a board or in the joist below it?

repair_options.method: Structural repair - add joist or sister the failing joist. Engineer assessment first.
Replace the individual board.

when_to_call_professional: If uncertain whether the crack is board-only or structural.
safety_note: If bounce accompanies the crack, stop use of the landing until inspected.

symptom: Floating staircase cantilever bracket appears to be pulling out of wall

possible_causes.cause: Wall structure inadequate for cantilever load
possible_causes.why: Bracket was fixed to wall that cannot carry cantilever moment - fixings pulling out.

possible_causes.cause: Fixings undersized for design load
possible_causes.why: Insufficient number or size of structural bolts.

repair_options.method: Structural engineer assessment required. Cantilever stairs need structural inspection - never a DIY fix.

when_to_call_professional: Immediately.
safety_note: Stop using the staircase. Cantilever failure can be sudden and complete.

symptom: Gap between staircase and wall has opened over time

possible_causes.cause: Building movement (subsidence or settlement)
possible_causes.why: The building has moved; the staircase is fixed to the floor, not the wall.

possible_causes.cause: Original install left small gap that seasonal movement has enlarged
possible_causes.why: Marginal initial fit has revealed itself over years.

diagnostic_questions.q: Are other parts of the house showing new cracks?

repair_options.method: Fill with decorator's caulk, paint over. Cosmetic only.
Structural surveyor - understand cause before treating symptom.

when_to_call_professional: If accompanied by other signs of building movement, call a surveyor.

symptom: Concrete stair edge chipping

possible_causes.cause: Freeze-thaw damage (external stairs)
possible_causes.why: Water penetrated concrete, froze, spalled the edges.

possible_causes.cause: Impact damage
possible_causes.why: Heavy objects dropped on edge.

possible_causes.cause: Poor concrete mix
possible_causes.why: Original concrete was under-strength.

repair_options.method: Chip out loose material back to sound concrete. Apply bonding agent. Rebuild edge with concrete repair mortar. Seal against water penetration.

when_to_call_professional: If large sections are failing, or exposed reinforcement is visible - call structural repair specialist.
safety_note: Broken concrete edges are trip hazards - mark or restrict access until repaired.

symptom: Steel stringer showing rust bloom

possible_causes.cause: Coating breakdown (external or moist environment)
possible_causes.why: Powder coat or paint has broken down; moisture is corroding underlying steel.

diagnostic_questions.q: Is the rust surface bloom, or has it eaten into the steel?

repair_options.method: Wire-brush rust back to bright metal, apply rust converter, prime and repaint with metal paint.
Structural inspection - may need welded repair or replacement.

when_to_call_professional: If rust is deep, or the stair carries significant load.
safety_note: External stairs with visible rust should be inspected before heavy use.

symptom: Trimmer joist above stair opening cracked

possible_causes.cause: Undersized joist for the trimmer load
possible_causes.why: Joist carries stair load plus floor load above - cannot handle both if under-specified.

possible_causes.cause: Cut or notch weakened joist during services install
possible_causes.why: Electrical or plumbing cut through the joist; failure over time.

repair_options.method: Structural engineer inspection mandatory. Sister the joist, replace, or reinforce as engineer specifies.

when_to_call_professional: Immediately.
safety_note: A cracked trimmer supports the stair opening AND the floor above. Stop use of both until inspected.

symptom: Cantilever tread has visible deflection

possible_causes.cause: Steel cantilever pin bending under load
possible_causes.why: The steel pin embedded in the wall is not strong enough for the tread load.

possible_causes.cause: Wall structure cannot resist cantilever moment
possible_causes.why: The wall itself is deflecting where the pin embeds.

repair_options.method: Structural engineer assessment. Cantilever staircases are engineered products - repair is engineer-led.

when_to_call_professional: Immediately.
safety_note: Stop using the affected step. Cantilever tread failure risks a fall from height.

symptom: Wall fixing bolt turning without tightening

possible_causes.cause: Wall plug has failed in the wall
possible_causes.why: The plastic plug has stripped its grip in the substrate.

possible_causes.cause: Fixing is only in plasterboard
possible_causes.why: The bolt was never in structural wall - just plasterboard behind.

repair_options.method: Remove bolt and plug. Use larger plug for oversized hole, or resin-fix the fixing into masonry with chemical anchor.
Longer fixing to reach structural wall behind. If no timber or masonry behind, use spring-toggle or heavy-duty plasterboard fixing - but this is not appropriate for handrail support (see diag-052).

when_to_call_professional: If fixing supports a handrail or safety-critical component, use a professional.

symptom: Handrail bracket fixed only into plasterboard

possible_causes.cause: Original install missed the structural stud
possible_causes.why: Fixing was made into plasterboard alone - will pull out under handrail load.

repair_options.method: Locate the structural stud (stud detector), remove bracket, refix into stud with 75mm+ structural screws. Or install a horizontal timber pattress screwed into the studs and mount brackets to that.

when_to_call_professional: If unsure how to locate structural fixing points, call an installer.
safety_note: A handrail fixed only to plasterboard will fail under fall-catch load. Warn users not to depend on it until refixed.

symptom: Screw head has stripped and cannot be removed

possible_causes.cause: Wrong driver bit or over-tightening
possible_causes.why: Bit slipped or cammed out under torque.

repair_options.method: Try a screw extractor bit designed for stripped heads. If that fails, drill out the screw head, remove component, extract remaining shank with mole grips or drill out.

when_to_call_professional: If the screw is in a difficult-to-reach location or the component around it might be damaged.

symptom: Newel bolt visible and rusting

possible_causes.cause: Original bolt was not concealed or not stainless
possible_causes.why: Steel bolt in a damp environment has surface-rusted.

repair_options.method: Wire-brush rust off, apply rust converter, prime and paint. Or replace with stainless bolt and conceal with a plug or filler.

when_to_call_professional: If concealment is not achievable easily.

symptom: Concealed screw is pushing up through finished tread

possible_causes.cause: Screw too long for material thickness
possible_causes.why: Installer chose oversized screw; timber movement has pushed it further.

possible_causes.cause: Filler over screw head has failed
possible_causes.why: Filler cap has fallen out; screw head visible.

repair_options.method: Remove screw, replace with shorter one. Fill hole, refinish.
Refill with matching wood filler, refinish.

when_to_call_professional: If multiple screws are affected - could indicate systemic install issue.
safety_note: Protruding screw head is a foot injury risk in bare-foot use.

symptom: Structural adhesive letting go under a floating tread

possible_causes.cause: Wrong adhesive spec for the load
possible_causes.why: Non-structural adhesive was used where structural was required.

possible_causes.cause: Contamination of bonding faces at install
possible_causes.why: Dust or oil on face during install has degraded the bond.

repair_options.method: Structural repair - remove, clean, re-bond with correct structural epoxy or engineered fixing. Installer only.

when_to_call_professional: Immediately.
safety_note: Do not use the affected tread until fixed. A floating stair failing without warning is a fall from height.

symptom: Pin popped through tread surface after install

possible_causes.cause: Timber movement has ejected the pin
possible_causes.why: Timber shrinkage has pushed the pin proud.

repair_options.method: Punch pin below surface with nail punch. Fill and refinish that spot.

when_to_call_professional: Only if widespread.
safety_note: Protruding pin is a bare-foot injury risk.

symptom: String fixing to trimmer joist has loosened

possible_causes.cause: Original fixing insufficient for load and cycling
possible_causes.why: Nails or short screws have loosened over years - the stair-to-house connection is failing.

repair_options.method: Installer to re-fix stringer to trimmer with structural screws or bolts of correct spec.

when_to_call_professional: Immediately.
safety_note: A stringer no longer connected to the trimmer is a whole-flight failure risk. Stop use.

symptom: Balustrade fixing bolt cover is missing

possible_causes.cause: Cover cap knocked off or vibrated loose
possible_causes.why: Small aesthetic cover not glued at install; has fallen out.

repair_options.method: Order replacement cap from the balustrade supplier (they are cheap). Push in - can add small dot of silicone if constantly falling out.

when_to_call_professional: Not needed.

symptom: Handrail wall bracket has come away with plaster attached

possible_causes.cause: Fixing was only in plasterboard/plaster - not structural
possible_causes.why: Bracket relied on plasterboard grip alone; catch-load has ripped it out.

repair_options.method: Repair plaster patch. Refix bracket into structural stud or masonry with 75mm+ structural screws and correct plugs. Or install timber pattress across studs first.

when_to_call_professional: If unsure of stud locations or comfortable working on plaster.
safety_note: Do not rely on the handrail until refixed. Warn all household members.

symptom: Cupped tread (edges higher than middle)

possible_causes.cause: Solid tread has cupped from moisture differential
possible_causes.why: One face has taken on/released moisture differently - the board has cupped.

diagnostic_questions.q: Is only the top face finished (unsealed underside)?

answer_maps_to.Yes: Moisture imbalance - both faces need sealing
answer_maps_to.No: Wide solid board reaching movement limit

repair_options.method: Seal the underside of the tread with matching finish (access from below). May allow the tread to re-flatten over months as moisture equalises.
Replace tread - preferably with engineered or laminated construction that resists cupping.

when_to_call_professional: If cup depth is more than 3-4mm - it becomes a trip hazard.
safety_note: A significantly cupped tread is a trip risk. Consider a temporary anti-slip cover until repaired.

symptom: Wide gap has opened between tread and skirting in winter

possible_causes.cause: Normal seasonal shrinkage
possible_causes.why: Central heating dries timber; gaps open in winter and close in summer.

diagnostic_questions.q: Does the gap close again in summer?

repair_options.method: If seasonal: do nothing, or add hallway humidifier. If permanent: fill with decorator's caulk.

when_to_call_professional: Not needed for seasonal movement.

symptom: Hairline crack running down a riser

possible_causes.cause: Timber shrinkage in wide solid riser
possible_causes.why: Wide solid boards develop shrinkage cracks in dry conditions - normal for solid timber.

repair_options.method: Fill with flexible wood filler that accepts finish. Refinish.

when_to_call_professional: Not needed unless the crack is significant or spreading.

symptom: Veneer lifting at edge of engineered tread

possible_causes.cause: Bond failure at edge
possible_causes.why: Original glue bond has failed, usually from water ingress at the edge.

possible_causes.cause: Moisture damage to substrate
possible_causes.why: The MDF or plywood core has swollen, pushing the veneer up.

repair_options.method: Small area: lift the loose veneer carefully, work in wood glue, press down and clamp with weight. Refinish.
Replace the tread - substrate cannot be un-swollen.

when_to_call_professional: If more than a small area is lifting.

symptom: Tread has bowed lengthwise (banana shape)

possible_causes.cause: Grain-direction issue in solid tread
possible_causes.why: Original board had grain running in a direction that encouraged bowing.

possible_causes.cause: Moisture imbalance between top and bottom
possible_causes.why: One face gaining/losing moisture faster than the other.

repair_options.method: Bowing rarely reverses. Replace tread with engineered or better-selected solid stock.

when_to_call_professional: Yes.
safety_note: A bowed tread is a trip risk if the bow is significant.

symptom: Knots are cracking and dropping out of pine treads

possible_causes.cause: Loose knots in original pine stock
possible_causes.why: Pine can have loose knots that eventually drop; normal for cheaper stock.

repair_options.method: Fill knot hole with two-part epoxy wood filler or a matching plug. Sand and refinish.

when_to_call_professional: If knot holes are on wearing surfaces and impact durability.

symptom: Timber has darkened where sun exposure ended
customer_language: patch on stairs where rug was

possible_causes.cause: UV exposure elsewhere lightened surrounding timber
possible_causes.why: Everything except the covered patch has faded - the patch is not dark, everything else is light.

repair_options.method: Expose the whole area to daylight; over months the tone often equalises. Or lightly sand and match with stain if immediate result needed.

when_to_call_professional: Not usually.

symptom: Two matched treads have taken on different colours over time

possible_causes.cause: Natural colour variation revealed by ageing
possible_causes.why: Two boards from the same tree age slightly differently; small original mismatch has grown with UV and use.

repair_options.method: Refinish both treads with a slight stain to blend colour, or accept as natural timber character.

when_to_call_professional: For serious mismatch on premium stairs, workshop refinish is best.

symptom: Squeaks appearing 2-3 months after new install

possible_causes.cause: Timber acclimatising and shrinking in the house environment
possible_causes.why: Workshop-conditioned timber has adjusted to the dryer house environment; small gaps have opened at joints.

repair_options.method: Contact the installer under warranty. Squeaks in the first 6-12 months are a known adjustment period - a good installer will return to re-wedge or re-fix.

when_to_call_professional: Yes - this is a warranty visit, not a homeowner-DIY job.

symptom: Newel post has developed a lengthwise crack

possible_causes.cause: Solid timber newel shrinkage crack
possible_causes.why: Large solid section drying and shrinking - crack relieves the stress.

diagnostic_questions.q: Is the crack cosmetic (surface only), or does it feel like the newel is weakened?

repair_options.method: Fill with wood filler or flexible caulk if cosmetic. If crack widens under load, replace newel.

when_to_call_professional: If the newel feels weaker or wobbles when pressed.

symptom: Multiple spindles have come loose in the baserail

possible_causes.cause: Slips have shrunk and released
possible_causes.why: Timber slips between spindles have shrunk with age; grip on the spindles has released.

possible_causes.cause: Original glue joints failing on age
possible_causes.why: Old-style glue on spindle bottoms has failed.

repair_options.method: Systematically re-glue and re-pin every spindle top and bottom. Refit or replace slips with fresh glue. Working through the whole flight is a day-long job but low skill.

when_to_call_professional: If the whole balustrade needs professional refit for aesthetic quality.
safety_note: A balustrade with multiple loose spindles is a fall risk - do not lean on it until repaired.

symptom: Glass balustrade panels not aligned at top

possible_causes.cause: Bosses drilled off-centre in glass at manufacture
possible_causes.why: Fixing holes not symmetrical; panels sit at slight angles.

possible_causes.cause: Channel not perfectly level at install
possible_causes.why: Setting-out error at install; every subsequent panel inherits the error.

repair_options.method: Glass specialist to loosen fixings, reset panels level, retighten. May require removing and re-drilling if bosses are wrong.

when_to_call_professional: Yes - glass work is not DIY.

symptom: Cable balustrade has visibly slack cables

possible_causes.cause: Cables have stretched with age
possible_causes.why: Stainless cable can stretch under sustained tension - most systems have adjustable tensioners.

repair_options.method: Locate cable tensioners (usually at one end - screw-adjusted or wrench-adjusted). Tighten each cable until it deflects less than 15mm under normal hand pressure. Doc K rule: gap must stay under 100mm even with cable pressed.

when_to_call_professional: If tensioners are seized or unable to remove all slack.
safety_note: Slack cables can allow a 100mm sphere to pass - child safety failure. Adjust promptly.

symptom: Wooden balustrade has developed 100mm+ gap between spindles

possible_causes.cause: Spindle has fallen out entirely
possible_causes.why: Loose spindle now missing - gap has doubled.

possible_causes.cause: Original spacing was non-compliant
possible_causes.why: Older stair built before current regs - never met the 100mm rule.

repair_options.method: Source matching spindle, refit into groove with glue and slips.
Add additional spindles between existing ones - joinery job for a carpenter.

when_to_call_professional: For non-compliant spacing on a stair with children in the household.
safety_note: A 100mm+ gap on a stair balustrade is a serious child-safety issue. Restrict child access to the stair until repaired.

symptom: Metal balustrade has developed rust at the base

possible_causes.cause: Coating breakdown at base where cleaning water pools
possible_causes.why: Powder coat broken at the foot; moisture from cleaning has corroded steel.

repair_options.method: Wire-brush rust, apply rust converter, prime and repaint with matching metal paint. Prevention: change cleaning routine to avoid pooling water at balustrade base.

when_to_call_professional: For extensive rust or if refurbishment is needed.

symptom: Glass panel has cracked but not broken

possible_causes.cause: Impact damage causing crack propagation
possible_causes.why: Toughened glass usually shatters completely on impact; a persistent crack is unusual and unstable.

possible_causes.cause: Edge damage propagating under thermal or mechanical stress
possible_causes.why: Latent edge chip has grown into face crack.

repair_options.method: Replace panel. Toughened glass cannot be repaired.

when_to_call_professional: Immediately.
safety_note: A cracked toughened panel can shatter suddenly and completely. Do not lean on or touch the panel. Restrict access.

symptom: Handrail groove is holding spindles but slips have popped out

possible_causes.cause: Original slips not glued at manufacture
possible_causes.why: Some builders only fit slips without glue - they eventually fall out.

repair_options.method: Cut new slips to length from matching timber. Glue and pin in position.

when_to_call_professional: Not needed.

symptom: Balustrade is warm to touch during summer

possible_causes.cause: Metal or dark-coloured components absorbing solar heat
possible_causes.why: Black metal in direct sun heats up - normal behaviour, not a defect.

repair_options.method: Not a repairable defect. Blinds or window film on the stairwell window reduce direct sun exposure if the temperature becomes uncomfortable.

when_to_call_professional: Not needed.

symptom: Glass panel channel is filling with dust and debris

possible_causes.cause: Normal accumulation over time
possible_causes.why: Any channel collects debris - needs periodic cleaning.

repair_options.method: Use a soft brush and vacuum to clear debris from the channel. Wipe with damp microfibre.

when_to_call_professional: Not needed.

symptom: Spindles look tilted (not vertical)

possible_causes.cause: Slips have shifted spindle position
possible_causes.why: Loose slips have let spindles move sideways in the groove.

possible_causes.cause: Building settlement
possible_causes.why: House movement has racked the balustrade.

repair_options.method: Reset spindles to vertical, glue and refit slips to lock position.

when_to_call_professional: If accompanied by other signs of building movement.

symptom: Handrail is loose at one end only

possible_causes.cause: Newel at that end is loose (see diag-011)
possible_causes.why: Handrail movement inherited from a loose newel.

possible_causes.cause: Handrail-to-newel joint failed
possible_causes.why: The specific fixing at that end has slackened.

diagnostic_questions.q: Does the newel itself move when pushed sideways?

repair_options.method: See diag-011.
Access joint fixing through newel top under the cap. Tighten or add hidden reinforcement screw.

when_to_call_professional: For hidden joint reinforcement, install an experienced carpenter.
safety_note: Warn users not to depend on the handrail at that end until repaired.

symptom: Handrail has a visible gap where two lengths join

possible_causes.cause: Timber shrinkage has opened the joint
possible_causes.why: Original joint was tight; seasonal drying has opened it.

possible_causes.cause: Original joint not glued
possible_causes.why: Installer relied on friction fit - joint has come apart.

repair_options.method: Clean joint faces, apply wood glue, clamp closed. If joint cannot be pulled fully closed, fill remaining hairline with matching wood filler.

when_to_call_professional: For premium handrails where visible repair is unacceptable.

symptom: Wall handrail is set too low or too high

possible_causes.cause: Original install did not follow regs
possible_causes.why: Domestic Doc K requires 900-1000mm above pitch line - install error.

repair_options.method: Refix brackets at correct height (900-1000mm above pitch line for domestic). Fill old holes and touch up. If handrail also needs replacing (length change), carpenter job.

when_to_call_professional: For neat refit and to confirm the correct regulation height.
safety_note: Wrong-height handrails are less effective in a fall - should be corrected on new installs under warranty.

symptom: Handrail is uncomfortable to grip - too fat or too thin

possible_causes.cause: Handrail profile does not match ergonomic guidance
possible_causes.why: Handrail should be 45-50mm diameter (round) or equivalent - some designs prioritise looks over grip.

repair_options.method: Replace handrail with correct-profile section. Cannot be modified in place.

when_to_call_professional: Yes.
safety_note: Non-graspable handrails do not perform their fall-catch function - correct if used by elderly or unsteady household members.

symptom: Only one side of the stair has a handrail

possible_causes.cause: Original install to old spec (one-sided handrail was standard)
possible_causes.why: Older stairs often had only wall-side handrails; balustrade handrails are the modern standard.

diagnostic_questions.q: Is the stair wider than 1000mm, or used by elderly or accessibility users?

answer_maps_to.No: Existing single handrail may be sufficient

repair_options.method: Install a second handrail on the wall side at 900-1000mm above pitch line. Standard bracket fitting into structural wall.

when_to_call_professional: For confidence in structural fixings.
safety_note: Both-side handrails significantly improve fall recovery for older users - worth doing regardless of regs.

symptom: Different riser heights within the same flight

possible_causes.cause: Manufacture or install error
possible_causes.why: Doc K requires all risers within 5mm of each other; larger variation is an install defect.

possible_causes.cause: Floor covering added after install
possible_causes.why: New flooring at top or bottom has changed the effective rise of the first or last step.

diagnostic_questions.q: Was flooring added at top or bottom after the stair was built?

repair_options.method: Requires stair rebuild or specific step modification - installer only.
Reduce covering at problem step, or add matching thickness to other steps.

when_to_call_professional: Yes.
safety_note: Uneven riser heights are the leading cause of stair fall injuries. Warn all users, prioritise repair.

symptom: I hit my head coming up the stairs

possible_causes.cause: Sloped ceiling / low ceiling reduces headroom below Doc K minimum
possible_causes.why: Doc K requires 2000mm minimum headroom vertically above the pitch line - hit-head indicates non-compliance.

possible_causes.cause: Loft conversion or extension has changed ceiling above stair
possible_causes.why: Post-original works have reduced the space.

repair_options.method: Structural change required - raising ceiling, moving stair, or accepting the limitation. Architect or structural engineer needed.

when_to_call_professional: Yes.
safety_note: Head-strike hazard is a real risk. Consider padded corner or clearly-marked warning until permanently resolved.

symptom: Stair pitch feels too steep for comfort

possible_causes.cause: Pitch exceeds Doc K 42-degree domestic maximum
possible_causes.why: Older stairs may exceed current pitch limit.

possible_causes.cause: Compliant but steep end of range
possible_causes.why: 42-degree stair is legal but feels steep to some users.

repair_options.method: Rebuild required - only feasible during major renovation.
Not a repair - user education and possibly both-side handrails to improve grip.

when_to_call_professional: For non-compliant pitch or if elderly users cannot manage.
safety_note: Steep stairs increase fall risk - improve lighting, add second handrail, consider stairlift if user needs it.

symptom: Tread going is too shallow for a full foot

possible_causes.cause: Going below Doc K 220mm minimum
possible_causes.why: Older or space-saving stairs may have going less than 220mm.

repair_options.method: Cannot be modified in place - the stair envelope is fixed by the opening. Only a full rebuild changes it.

when_to_call_professional: For renovation-scale response.
safety_note: Descending is more dangerous than ascending on shallow-going stairs. Warn users, add both-side handrails, consider nosing grip strips.

symptom: Nosing overhang seems missing or damaged

possible_causes.cause: Original design without overhang (modern square-edge)
possible_causes.why: Not a defect - modern stairs often have square edges intentionally.

possible_causes.cause: Overhang cut off in past repair
possible_causes.why: Damaged nosing was cut back rather than replaced.

repair_options.method: Not a repair - accept the design choice.
Add applied nosing strip - joinery job.

when_to_call_professional: For applied nosing.

symptom: Skirting board stops abruptly at the string with gap or bad mitre

possible_causes.cause: String was not prepared to receive skirting at manufacture
possible_causes.why: See brain entry 1838 - skirting coordination requires pre-manufacture communication.

repair_options.method: Fill gap with decorator's caulk matched to paint colour. Cosmetic only.
Carpenter to add a scribed timber block or trim to disguise the joint.

when_to_call_professional: For premium stairs where cosmetic caulk is unacceptable.

symptom: Visible unfilled pin holes across finished tread surface

possible_causes.cause: Installer did not fill pins before finish
possible_causes.why: Skipped step in the finishing process.

repair_options.method: Fill each pin hole with matching wood filler using a small applicator. Touch up finish over each spot.

when_to_call_professional: If on a new install, installer should return under warranty.

symptom: Finish is contaminated with dust and specks

possible_causes.cause: Finish applied without dust control
possible_causes.why: Site-applied lacquer or on-site sanding dust settled in wet finish.

repair_options.method: Full re-finish under proper dust control - workshop spray booth if possible.

when_to_call_professional: Yes.

symptom: Fresh install has visible dents from clamps or pipe presses

possible_causes.cause: Installer clamped over finished timber without protection
possible_causes.why: Direct clamp contact has crushed timber fibre.

repair_options.method: Steam-raise the crushed fibre - damp cloth and hot iron. Fill remainder with wood filler. Refinish that spot.

when_to_call_professional: New install - installer to correct under warranty.

symptom: Stair has been installed out of square with the wall

possible_causes.cause: Install error - not levelled and squared before fixing
possible_causes.why: Wall was not straight, installer did not compensate with packers.

repair_options.method: Installer to unfix, re-set with correct packing, re-fix. Not a small job.

when_to_call_professional: Yes - warranty issue.

symptom: No lighting cable was routed for planned LED strip

possible_causes.cause: Lighting not planned before install (see brain 1849)
possible_causes.why: Cable route needed during first-fix; retrofit means visible trunking or destructive access.

repair_options.method: Options: (1) surface-mount LED strip with cable in a discreet trunking - fastest and cheapest. (2) Battery-operated LED strips with charging dock hidden - no cable at all. (3) Partial disassembly of the stair to run cable - most invasive.

when_to_call_professional: For cable running inside finished stair components.

symptom: Wall behind stair was not fully plastered before install

possible_causes.cause: Trade sequencing error - stair before plaster
possible_causes.why: Should have been plastered first - the stair now blocks access.

repair_options.method: Plaster the visible parts of the wall, accepting that behind-stair sections may need to remain as bare plasterboard. Careful masking of finished timber essential.

when_to_call_professional: For plaster work.

symptom: Newel is standing on subfloor rather than finished floor

possible_causes.cause: Stair fitted before finished floor - not accounted for
possible_causes.why: See brain entry 1810 - finished floor level must be known before install.

repair_options.method: Add a base moulding or plinth to hide the gap. If gap is severe, newel may need lifting and re-fixing (installer job).

when_to_call_professional: For significant gap requiring newel modification.
safety_note: If the gap has weakened the newel base fixing, address as loose newel (diag-011).

symptom: Handover paperwork was never provided

possible_causes.cause: Installer did not include handover pack (unprofessional practice)
possible_causes.why: Premium installers provide printed care instructions, warranty, maintenance schedule, CAD drawing (see brain 1817).

repair_options.method: Request in writing from the installer. Any professional installer will provide it. Keep the email trail as your warranty evidence.

when_to_call_professional: Request from the original installer.

symptom: Multiple visible defects on a brand-new installation

possible_causes.cause: Systemic install quality failure
possible_causes.why: Multiple defects together indicate a wider quality problem, not a single mistake.

repair_options.method: Do not attempt individual DIY repairs on a new install with multiple defects. Follow the poorly-fitted staircase protocol (see brain entries 1783-1792): document everything, contact installer in writing, request full inspection, escalate if refused.

when_to_call_professional: This is a warranty issue and potentially a Consumer Rights Act 2015 case. Follow the escalation route in the brain, not the DIY route.
safety_note: If any defect is safety-critical (loose handrail, loose newel, cracked stringer), stop use of the affected part immediately and prioritise those defects in the inspection request.
